biblical_def: Tahath is a station of the children of Israel in the wilderness, named in the itinerary of their journeys which Moses wrote at the commandment of the LORD (Num 33:26-27). They encamped there coming from Makheloth, and from Tahath they departed and pitched at Tarah. The name signifies “beneath” or “a station set under,” from a common Hebrew word for that which is below or in the place of another. Of any event at Tahath the Scripture is silent; it is one of the many camps in the long road of the forty years, set down by name that the goings of Israel might be known. The Most High set them under His mighty hand, that He might exalt them in due time. Tahath stands as a witness that the LORD leads His people through low places and humbling stations, that they may learn to lean wholly upon Him; for it is the way of God to bring His own beneath His hand of discipline before He lifts them up in due time.

biblical_def: Hashmonah is a station of the children of Israel in the wilderness, recorded by Moses in the itinerary of their journeys which he wrote at the commandment of the LORD (Num 33:29-30). etymology: Hebrew moseroth, “bonds” or “chastisements,” the plural from a root meaning to bind or to instruct, called also Mosera, a station of Israel near where Aaron died.
biblical_def: Moseroth, called also Mosera, is a station of the children of Israel in the wilderness, named in the itinerary which Moses wrote at the commandment of the LORD (Num 33:30-31), and it is by Mosera that Deuteronomy records the death of Aaron and the mourning of the people (Deu 10:6). They came to Moseroth from Hashmonah, and from Moseroth they removed and pitched in Bene-jaakan. The name signifies “bonds” or “chastisements,” from a root that speaks both of binding and of instruction, for the chastening of the LORD is His instruction unto His sons. It was near this place, at mount Hor by the coast of Edom, that Aaron the high priest was gathered to his people, and the congregation wept for him thirty days; and the dictionary honours that the very name of the station spoke of bonds and discipline, for it was here that Israel felt the bond of mortality even upon their high priest, who could not pass into the land for the sin at the waters of strife. There is a solemn grace here, for Aaron’s priesthood could not continue by reason of death, but pointed onward to the Lord Jesus, who hath an unchangeable priesthood. Moseroth stands as a witness that the chastisements of the LORD are the bonds of His love, and that He who taketh away the mortal priest hath given us an High Priest who ever liveth to make intercession and to save to the uttermost.

etymology: Hebrew bene ya‘aqan, “sons of Jaakan” or “children of Jaakan,” called also Beeroth of the children of Jaakan, the wells of the sons of Jaakan, a station of Israel in the wilderness.
biblical_def: Bene-jaakan, the children of Jaakan, is a station of Israel in the wilderness, named in the itinerary which Moses wrote at the commandment of the LORD (Num 33:31-32), and called in Deuteronomy Beeroth of the children of Jaakan, that is, the wells of the sons of Jaakan (Deu 10:6). They came thither from Moseroth, and from Bene-jaakan they removed and pitched in Hor-hagidgad. Jaakan was a son of Ezer the Horite, of the dwellers in mount Seir, so that the place bore the name of an Edomite clan whose wells gave water in that dry land. Of any event at Bene-jaakan the Scripture is silent, save that here was water, the wells of Jaakan, in the midst of the great and terrible wilderness wherein there was no water. The dictionary honours the providence that brought the thirsting host to the wells of Jaakan, for the LORD who led them through the waste knew every spring and every cistern, and He guided them to water as He had given them water out of the rock of flint. It is no small mercy that the camps of the wandering should be remembered by their wells, for the LORD is the fountain of living waters to His people. Bene-jaakan stands as a witness that He who led Israel to the wells of Jaakan leads His thirsting church to the springs of His salvation, and bids all that are athirst come unto Him and drink, that they may never thirst again.

etymology: Hebrew chor haggidgad, “the cavern of Gidgad” or “the hollow of the cleft,” called also Gudgodah, a station of Israel in the wilderness wandering.
biblical_def: Hor-hagidgad, called also Gudgodah, is a station of the children of Israel in the wilderness, named in the itinerary which Moses wrote at the commandment of the LORD (Num 33:32-33), and remembered in Deuteronomy as Gudgodah, whither the people journeyed from Bene-jaakan (Deu 10:7). They came to it from Bene-jaakan, and from Hor-hagidgad they removed and pitched in Jotbathah, which Moses calls a land of rivers of waters. The name signifies “the cavern of Gidgad” or “the hollow of the cleft,” speaking of some hollow or ravine in that broken country. Of any event at Hor-hagidgad the Scripture is silent; it is a name in the long road of the forty years, set down that the goings of Israel might be known and remembered. Yet the dictionary honours that the Spirit of God recorded even this obscure cleft, for the LORD who led His people knew every hollow of the waste, and not one station was hidden from His eye. He led them about and kept them as the apple of His eye, and from the cleft of Gudgodah He brought them on toward the land of rivers of waters. Hor-hagidgad stands as a witness that the way of the LORD with His people runs through clefts and broken places, yet leads ever on toward the springs and the rest He has prepared, for He who hideth His own in the cleft of the rock will bring them at the last unto the city whose builder and maker is God.
